what_happened: First scratch-repo setup command used 'git add -A' inside a heredoc targeting an unrelated scratch repo; guard-destructive-git.sh's PreToolUse Bash hook blocked the whole command on substring match alone (no cwd/target-repo discrimination), so none of that call's setup ran. Worse: the next chained command's 'cd' into the (still-nonexistent) scratch repo silently failed and fell through to the live nvim repo's cwd, where a subsequent 'git worktree add' then ran for real, attaching a throwaway worktree+branch to the production repo. Cleaned up immediately with git worktree remove --force and git branch -D. Rebuilt the scratch fixture with explicit file staging and strict && chaining.

Decisively measured guard-destructive-git.sh's hook-cwd anchor live: committed a scratch git-worktree (sited outside the project directory) to a fully clean state, then ran 'cd <clean external worktree> && git reset --hard HEAD' in one Bash call. The command was BLOCKED with a message citing 'uncommitted changes' even though the actual cd-target tree was clean -- proving the hook's safety decision is anchored to the primary project tree's own git status, not to the Bash command's own cwd target. This independently reconfirms, from the opposite direction, the already-recorded finding that guard-destructive-git.sh judges safety from its own process directory rather than the command's real target.
